name: Mexico's cartel war (CJNG succession fight and Sinaloa Cartel civil war)
started: 2024-09-09 (start of the Sinaloa Cartel civil war; CJNG succession crisis from 2026-02-22)
summary: Mexico's war against and among drug cartels entered a new phase when the army killed CJNG leader 'El Mencho' on 22 February 2026, setting off about 250 to 280 burning roadblocks across some 20 states. In Sinaloa, the civil war between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos passed two years in September 2026 with about 3,724 murders and about 4,000 people disappeared. Official national homicide figures have nonetheless fallen by roughly half since 2024.

sides.name: Mexican state
members: Secretariat of National Defense (SEDENA): Mexican Army, including the Joint Special Operations Command (FEC), Special Forces and the Brigada de Fusileros Paracaidistas
Security Ministry (SSPC) under Omar García Harfuch; state police forces
backers: United States (intelligence and planning support through Joint Interagency Task Force-Counter Cartel)
leaders: Gen. Ricardo Trevilla Trejo (Secretary of National Defense)
sides.strength: National Guard about 120,000 personnel (Wikipedia, National Guard (Mexico)); 200 elite troops sent to Sinaloa in late 2025 and a reported 1,600 more in Jan 2026 (Expansión Política, Feb 2026)

sides.name: Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación (CJNG)
members: CJNG regional cells in Jalisco, Michoacán, Guanajuato, Colima, Zacatecas and beyond
leaders: Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes 'El Mencho' (leader, killed 22 Feb 2026)
Juan Carlos Valencia González 'El Pelón' (reported successor, per WSJ and El País, Mar to Apr 2026)
Audias Flores Silva 'El Jardinero' (contender, captured 27 Apr 2026)
sides.strength: Not reliably estimated; operates in more than 60 countries and, per a 2024 DEA report, all 50 US states (LRB, Mar 2026)

sides.name: Sinaloa Cartel: Los Chapitos
members: Faction led by the sons of Joaquín 'El Chapo' Guzmán
sides.strength: Not estimated in the sources consulted

sides.name: Sinaloa Cartel: Los Mayos (Mayitos)
members: Faction loyal to Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada, who is jailed in the US
leaders: Ismael Zambada Sicairos 'El Mayito Flaco' (faction leader)
sides.strength: Not estimated in the sources consulted

sides.name: Local armed groups in Michoacán
members: Groups resisting CJNG in Tierra Caliente (Tepalcatepec, Coalcomán, Apatzingán)
sides.strength: Not estimated in the sources consulted

background: Mexico has fought organized crime with the armed forces since 2006, and the National Guard created in 2019 was placed under the Defense Ministry by a 2022 reform. Two developments define the current phase. First, in July 2024 Sinaloa Cartel co-founder Ismael 'El Mayo' Zambada was taken to the US, and on 9 September 2024 open war broke out between his faction (Los Mayos) and Los Chapitos, the sons of 'El Chapo' Guzmán, turning Culiacán into a battlefield. Second, the US designated the CJNG and Sinaloa Cartel as terrorist organizations in 2025 and threatened unilateral strikes, which President Sheinbaum has rejected. Since then Mexico has tried to show results on its own terms: transfers of jailed bosses to the US, more troops in hot spots and, in 2026, a raid that killed the country's most wanted man with US intelligence help.

These dynamics matter beyond Mexico because the CJNG holds the largest share of the US fentanyl and methamphetamine markets, and because the question of whether US forces strike inside Mexico is one of the most consequential security issues in the hemisphere.
year: In late 2025 the Sinaloa war ground on, with 1,654 homicides in the state in 2025 against 993 in 2024. In Michoacán, CJNG fought local groups for Tierra Caliente using drone-dropped explosives and buried mines; SEDENA says it has found 625 such devices since November 2025. In January 2026 ten workers from a Canadian mining company disappeared near Concordia, Sinaloa; five bodies were later identified, and the security secretary said they were mistaken for Mayos members.

On 22 February 2026, Army special forces and paratroopers backed by helicopters raided a gated estate in Tapalpa, Jalisco, using US intelligence. El Mencho was badly wounded and died en route to Mexico City. CJNG responded with about 250 roadblocks of burning vehicles, a car bomb in San Juan de los Lagos that killed an army captain, attacks on National Guard bases and a prison break near Puerto Vallarta. At least 25 National Guard members were killed in the following days; one account puts police and Guard deaths at 50 or more. Most roadblocks were cleared within 48 hours. His stepson 'El Pelón' was reported as the new leader by April, and rival contender 'El Jardinero' was captured on 27 April.

Through mid-2026 the government reported steep falls in homicides: 42.2 per day in September 2026 against 86.9 in September 2024, the lowest September since 2015. In Sinaloa, however, the war reached its second anniversary on 9 September 2026 with about 3,724 murders, around 4,000 people disappeared and about 7,000 businesses closed.
situation: As of late October 2026 Mexico reports its lowest homicide rates in a decade, but the Sinaloa civil war continues at about five killings a day, Sinaloa is the fourth-deadliest state, and Michoacán remains a mined and drone-contested front between CJNG and local groups. The CJNG has not visibly broken apart since El Mencho's death, but its leadership is contested. US pressure for direct action continues; no US strike on Mexican soil was found in the sources consulted.
technical: Tapalpa raid, 22 Feb 2026: SEDENA Joint Special Operations Command (FEC), Army Special Forces and the Brigada de Fusileros Paracaidistas, with Air Force and National Guard support; six helicopters pre-positioned, two in direct support; one hit by gunfire and forced down at Sayula (Wikipedia, 2026 Jalisco operation).
US role: the Joint Interagency Task Force-Counter Cartel (JIATF-CC) provided intelligence, mapped cartel presence and helped plan the Tapalpa raid.
CJNG retaliation: about 250 roadblocks nationwide (Wikipedia) or more than 280 on 24 Feb (LRB), built from hijacked trucks and buses set on fire; about 90 percent cleared by the evening of 23 Feb.

Retaliation weapons: a car bomb in San Juan de los Lagos killed Army Captain Leonel Cardoso Gómez; a vehicle bomb damaged a National Guard base; an armed assault hit the National Guard base at Teocaltiche.
Ixtapa prison (Puerto Vallarta area) assaulted on 22 Feb 2026: 23 inmates freed and a guard killed.
Guanajuato alone recorded more than 70 attacks in 23 municipalities, including arson on Banco del Bienestar branches and Oxxo stores.
Drone warfare: SEDENA logged 16 drone and IED attacks on soldiers from Feb to Oct 2025, mostly in Michoacán; analysts say many go unrecorded (EFE, Feb 2026).
Mines: SEDENA located 625 'narcominas' and drone-dropped explosives in Michoacán since Nov 2025, linked to the CJNG fight for Tepalcatepec, Coalcomán and Apatzingán (El Imparcial, Jul 2026).
Seized CJNG 'narconómina' payroll documents list payments to gunmen, lookouts and possibly police; authenticity under investigation by the FGR.
National Guard: about 120,000 personnel, under SEDENA command since a 2022 reform package.
Sinaloa troop surge: 200 elite troops in late 2025, with a reported 1,600 more arriving on 29 Jan 2026 (Expansión Política).

Homicide data: SESNSP counts 42.2 intentional homicides per day in Sep 2026, down from 86.9 in Sep 2024; seven states (Baja California, Guanajuato, Chihuahua, Sinaloa, Estado de México, Guerrero, Morelos) account for about half (Por Esto, 13 Oct 2026).
Sinaloa war cost: about 7,000 businesses closed and about 27,000 jobs lost by Sep 2026 (Coparmex Sinaloa via UnoTV).
casualties: Sinaloa civil war: 3,724 intentional homicides in Sinaloa from 9 Sep 2024 to early Sep 2026, about 5.1 per day (UnoTV, citing state security council, prosecutor and Coparmex, 7 Sep 2026); 1,654 in 2025 versus 993 in 2024 (Expansión Política, Feb 2026). Disappeared: about 4,000 in Sinaloa (Coparmex, Sep 2026); 2,320 reported and 1,445 still missing by Feb 2026 (national registry). Post-Mencho wave: at least 25 National Guard killed (Wikipedia, 2026 Jalisco operation); at least 50 police and Guard killed (LRB, Mar 2026); raid itself 7 to 8 CJNG dead and 3 security forces dead (infobox), with unconfirmed reports of higher military losses. National: 42.2 intentional homicides per day in Sep 2026 (SESNSP, preliminary). Homicide counts exclude the disappeared, so the true toll is higher.
displaced: Residents have left Sinaloa for Tijuana, Los Cabos, La Paz, Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey, but no total was found (UnoTV, Sep 2026).

timeline.event: Open war breaks out between Los Chapitos and Los Mayos in Sinaloa.
Ten Vizsla Silver mine workers disappear near Concordia, Sinaloa; five bodies later identified.
Army raid in Tapalpa, Jalisco, kills CJNG leader El Mencho; CJNG sets about 250 roadblocks and attacks security forces in multiple states.
More than 280 blockades reported across Mexico as violence peaks before subsiding.
Wall Street Journal reports El Mencho's stepson Juan Carlos Valencia González has taken over the CJNG.
CJNG commander Audias Flores Silva 'El Jardinero' captured.
Sinaloa war reaches two years with about 3,724 homicides and around 4,000 disappeared.
Government reports 42.2 homicides per day in September 2026, the lowest September since 2015.

outlook: Watch for a CJNG split or an internal purge as the succession settles, and for spillover into Guanajuato, Zacatecas and Colima. In Sinaloa, look for a decisive win by one faction or another high-level arrest. Spread of drone bombs and mines in Michoacán is the main tactical trend. The biggest wildcard is US action: Washington has designated both cartels as terrorist organizations and could push for direct strikes, which Mexico's government rejects.

zones.name: Culiacán and central Sinaloa
zones.note: Core battleground of the Chapitos versus Mayos war since Sep 2024; curfews, shootings and disappearances.

zones.name: Southern Sinaloa (Concordia and Mazatlán hinterland)
zones.note: Mining-area violence; ten Vizsla Silver workers disappeared in Jan 2026.

zones.name: Jalisco: Guadalajara metro and Tapalpa
zones.note: CJNG heartland; site of the El Mencho raid and the worst of the February 2026 roadblocks.

zones.name: Michoacán Tierra Caliente
zones.note: CJNG versus local groups around Apatzingán, Tepalcatepec and Coalcomán; drone bombs and buried mines.

zones.name: Guanajuato corridor
zones.note: Long the deadliest state; more than 70 attacks after El Mencho's death, though homicides fell sharply in 2026.

zones.name: Baja California (Tijuana)
zones.note: State with the largest share of national homicides in Jan to Sep 2026 (8.5 percent).

zones.name: Chihuahua (Ciudad Juárez)
zones.note: Third-highest share of national homicides in Jan to Sep 2026.

battles.name: Tapalpa raid (killing of 'El Mencho')
battles.place: Tapalpa Country Club, Tapalpa, Jalisco, Mexico
sides: Mexican Army and Air Force (with US intelligence support)
battles.outcome: CJNG leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes 'El Mencho' mortally wounded, dying en route to Mexico City; Rubén Guerrero Valadez also killed.
battles.forces: SEDENA Joint Special Operations Command (FEC), Army Special Forces and the Brigada de Fusileros Paracaidistas, Air Force and National Guard; six helicopters pre-positioned, two in direct support; US JIATF-CC intelligence and planning.
battles.losses: CJNG: 7 killed and 2 arrested (infobox) or 8 killed (Defence Secretary Trevilla); security forces: 3 killed (infobox); one helicopter hit and forced down at Sayula (Wikipedia, 2026 Jalisco operation).
battles.significance: Removed Mexico's most wanted trafficker and the founder of the CJNG, opening a succession fight in the largest supplier of fentanyl and methamphetamine to the US.

battles.name: CJNG blockade and retaliation wave
battles.place: Guadalajara metro area and about 20 states, centred on Jalisco, Guanajuato and Michoacán, Mexico
sides: Mexican Army, National Guard and state police
battles.outcome: About 250 roadblocks (more than 280 on 24 Feb by another count) were largely cleared within 48 hours; the state retained control but suffered heavy losses.
battles.forces: CJNG cells using hijacked and burned trucks and buses, car bombs and armed assaults on National Guard bases; Army and National Guard clearing operations.
battles.losses: At least 25 National Guard killed (Wikipedia) or at least 50 police and Guard killed (LRB); an Army captain killed by a car bomb in San Juan de los Lagos; a prison guard killed and 23 inmates freed at Ixtapa; dozens of suspected cartel members reported killed.
battles.significance: Showed the CJNG's ability to paralyse a region of Mexico within hours, and the cost of decapitation strikes.

battles.name: Abduction and killing of Vizsla Silver mine workers
battles.outcome: Ten workers of a Canadian mining company disappeared; five bodies later identified in El Verde, Concordia.
battles.forces: Armed cartel cell; the security secretary said the workers were mistaken for Mayos members.
battles.losses: At least 5 dead identified; others missing (Expansión Política, Feb 2026).
battles.significance: Showed the war's spread into southern Sinaloa's mining belt and its risk to foreign investment.

sources.label: Expansión Política: Más de 2,400 homicidios deja guerra en Sinaloa

battles.name: CJNG mine and drone campaign in Tierra Caliente
battles.place: Tepalcatepec, Coalcomán and Apatzingán, Michoacán, Mexico
sides: Local armed groups and Mexican Army
battles.outcome: Ongoing; SEDENA has cleared 625 mines and drone-dropped explosives since November 2025 (start date approximate).
battles.forces: Commercial drones modified to drop explosives, buried improvised mines; Army engineers and troops.
battles.losses: Not totalled in sources; SEDENA logged 16 drone and IED attacks on soldiers in Feb to Oct 2025, mostly in Michoacán (EFE).
battles.significance: Mexico's clearest example of cartels adopting battlefield technology, from mines to drone bombs, against soldiers and civilians.

sources.label: El Imparcial: Sedena ha localizado 625 narcominas y explosivos lanzados con drones en Michoacán
EFE via Expreso: Cárteles mexicanos intensifican ataques con drones

battles.name: Sinaloa Cartel civil war in Culiacán
battles.outcome: Ongoing; no faction has won after two years.
battles.forces: Cartel gunmen of both factions; Mexican Army and National Guard reinforced by 200 elite troops in late 2025 and a reported 1,600 more in Jan 2026.
battles.losses: 3,724 homicides in Sinaloa by Sep 2026 and about 4,000 disappeared (UnoTV, 7 Sep 2026).
battles.significance: The longest and deadliest internal war of a major Mexican cartel, gutting the economy of Sinaloa's capital.
